newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Levy summons Egyptian ambassador.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Levy summons Egyptian ambassador.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy summoned Egypt's ambassador, Mohammed Bassyouni, to a meeting on Tuesday after criticism of the Jewish state by Egypt.
Egypt's assistant foreign minister, Fathi el-Shazli, said on Monday Israeli leaders were talking like "dinosaurs" about the situation in the Middle East and were amateur politicians.
But Bassyouni told Reuters he was "sure that the media had misquoted Shazli". He said such statements contradicted Egyptian policy. "We only criticise policy. We do not attack individuals," he said.
Bassyouni said a foreign ministry official telephoned him on Monday and asked him to the meeting.
"I will meet with Levy at his office at 1100 (0900 GMT) in Jerusalem," he said. "I don't know yet what he will tell me but of course we will talk of relations between Egypt and Israel."
Israeli officials would not comment on what Levy would relay to Bassyouni.

However, an Israeli official, who did not want to be identified, reacted to the remarks made by Shazli, saying: "The statements allegedly used by the assistant foreign minister will not help Egypt be more respected among its partners."
Shazli was referring to an interview Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave the German Der Spiegel magazine in which he said there would never be a Palestinian state.
"The language used by Israeli officials is the language of dinosaurs, it goes against the logic of this age," Shazli said.
"This language provokes disgust because Israel is a party to what is called the peace process and it has obligations towards various other parties."
Netanyahu came to power in May on a platform that rejected the creation of a Palestinian state and promised a tougher line with Arab peace partners.
Shazli also referred to warnings Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai levelled at Syria over its troop movements in Lebanon.

"This banging of war drums by Israeli officials and the threat to resort to the military option will not help create the necessary groundwork for the success of any peace efforts because it will doubtless create equal reactions," he said.
Shazli's comments were among the strongest in a war of words brewing since Netanyahu won elections in May.
Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel but relations between the two countries over the years have often been strained.
